messages.subject: Question about validation
parts:
Hi,

I have a question regarding code for validating models using R-INLA-SPDE that I was hoping someone might be able to offer some advice. I am trying to validate a negative binomial model by comparing the predictions vs. the observed results of a subset of the data that was held out of the full dataset to be used for validation. 

I found the predicted vs. observed values of the validation dataset to be quite different. I was wondering if there is something wrong with the code I am using or if there is another method of validation that I could use? I read about sampling from the posterior distribution, but was not sure of how to interpret the output once I sampled from it and am unsure if it would produce  different results from what I have used with the method below.

The code and output are below.

Sincerely,

Kristin

The summary of predicted values and observed values from the code below are as follows: The correlation between the observed and predicted values was 0.40.

#Output from predictions made from validation dataset

     Min.         1st Qu.        Median      Mean           3rd Qu.          Max.

  0.079              3.89         10.54           17.02          22.62          237.45

#Output of observed values

   Min.            1st Qu.        Median     Mean             3rd Qu.           Max.

   0.00               0.00              3.00         18.56            13.00           2246.00



The code I have used is below:

Loc <- cbind(train$x, train$y)

Loc1 <- cbind(validation$x, validation$y)

ConvHull <- inla.nonconvex.hull(Loc, convex = 15000, concave = 20000)

Mesh3 <- inla.mesh.2d(boundary = ConvHull, max.edge = c(15000, 75000), cutoff = (3000), offset = c(15000, 75000))

A_est <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = Mesh3, loc = Loc)

A.pred <- inla.spde.make.A(mesh = Mesh3, loc = Loc1)

spde1 <- inla.spde2.matern(Mesh3, alpha = 2) 

spde1$n.spde 

s.index <- inla.spde.make.index(name = "spatial.field2", n.spde = spde1$n.spde)

dep.stack <- inla.stack(data  = list(Y = train$Y),

                        A = list(A_est, 1),

                        effects = list(c(s.index, list(Intercept=1)),

                                       list(A = train$A,

                                             B = train$B,

                                            C = train$C,

                                            D = train$D,

                                            E = train$E)),

                        tag = "Est")

dep.stack.pred <- inla.stack(data = list(Y = NA),

                             A = list(A.pred, 1),

                             effects = list(c(s.index, list (Intercept = 1)),

                                            list(A = validation$A,

                                                 B = validation$B,

                                                 C = validation$C,

                                                 D = validation$D,

                                                 E = validation$E)),

                             tag = "Valid")

 

join.stack <- inla.stack(dep.stack, dep.stack.pred)

U <- 0.01

hyper.prec <- list(theta = list (

  prior = "pc.prec",

  param = c(U, 0.05)))

form <- Y ~ -1 + Intercept + A + B + C +  

  f(spatial.field2, model = spde1) +  f(D, model = "rw2", hyper = hyper.prec) +                     f(E, model = "iid")     

Model   <- inla(form,

                   data = inla.stack.data(join.stack, spde = spde1),

                   family = "nbinomial",

                   inla.setOption(scale.model.default = TRUE),

                   inla.mode = "experimental",

                   control.inla = list(tolerance = 1e-10),

                   control.predictor = list(A = inla.stack.A(join.stack), compute = T, link=1))


#Make summary of predicted versus observed

index.test_CR <- inla.stack.index(join.stack, 'Valid')$data

summary(index.test_CR1)

summary(test_steps$Y)

 

#Calculate correlation between predicted and observed

cor(index.test_CR1, test_steps$Y)

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Question about validation
parts:
﻿
﻿
The﻿ linear predictor quantity (eta) and version transformed via the link function, typically controls the location parameter of the data distribution, so is never directly comparable to observations (y) without taking in account the variance and/or full distribution model.
Credible intervals (like confidence intervals) for eta do not incorporate the variability of the observations themselves; for that you need to take the full distribution into account, e.g. through predictive intervals on the data level itself. This is an extremely fundamental thing, but it appears this is not handled properly in teaching materials about regression and hierarchical models, since we see this confusion a lot. 

That’s why a common recommendation is to sample from the observation distribution conditionally on samples of the posterior for eta; it gives a Monte Carlo approximation of the distribution for each left out observation. For specific models one can often compute quantities more directly, e.g. instead of sampling y, use the sampled eta values to approximate the resulting mixture distribution pdf or pdf instead.
In the online inlabru package examples, we use that technique to estimate a predictive mixture of Poisson distributions, but direct sampling is simpler, and works the same for all models.

Finn

messages.subject: Re: [r-inla] Question about validation
parts:
As a further example, we can consider the overall variance of the left out observations, using the “tower property” of expectations:
For expectations,
E(y)=E(E(y|eta)),
so that the overall average is the average of the conditional expectations.
But for variances, this turns into two terms,
Var(y) = E(Var(y|eta)) + Var(E(y|eta)),
so that the variance is the average of the conditional variances, plus the variance of the conditional expectations. For regression models, the whole point is usually that eta is different for each observation  (and typically E(y|eta) = g^-1(eta) from the inverse link function) so both terms contribute to the overall variance of the observations.

Finn

> > As a further example, we can consider the overall variance of the
> > left out observations, using the “tower property” of expectations:
> > For expectations,
> > E(y)=E(E(y|eta)),
> > so that the overall average is the average of the conditional
> > expectations.
> > But for variances, this turns into two terms,
> > Var(y) = E(Var(y|eta)) + Var(E(y|eta)),
> > so that the variance is the average of the conditional variances,
> > plus the variance of the conditional expectations. For regression
> > models, the whole point is usually that eta is different for each
> > observation  (and typically E(y|eta) = g^-1(eta) from the inverse
> > link function) so both terms contribute to the overall variance of
> > the observations.
> >
> > Finn

> > > ﻿
> > > The﻿ linear predictor quantity (eta) and version transformed via
> > > the link function, typically controls the location parameter of
> > > the data distribution, so is never directly comparable to
> > > observations (y) without taking in account the variance and/or
> > > full distribution model.
> > > Credible intervals (like confidence intervals) for eta do not
> > > incorporate the variability of the observations themselves; for
> > > that you need to take the full distribution into account, e.g.
> > > through predictive intervals on the data level itself. This is an
> > > extremely fundamental thing, but it appears this is not handled
> > > properly in teaching materials about regression and hierarchical
> > > models, since we see this confusion a lot. 
> > >
> > > That’s why a common recommendation is to sample from the
> > > observation distribution conditionally on samples of the posterior
> > > for eta; it gives a Monte Carlo approximation of the distribution
> > > for each left out observation. For specific models one can often
> > > compute quantities more directly, e.g. instead of sampling y, use
> > > the sampled eta values to approximate the resulting mixture
> > > distribution pdf or pdf instead.
> > > In the online inlabru package examples, we use that technique to
> > > estimate a predictive mixture of Poisson distributions, but direct
> > > sampling is simpler, and works the same for all models.
> > >
